chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Financing an income property follows different rules from those of a house. Down payment, treatment of rental income, loan insurance: well structured, your financing can make or break the profitability of your project.

This guide covers the main rules (1 to 4 units vs 5 and more), the down payment, the role of loan-insurance programs, and the importance of a solid structure.

2026 editorial note: rules and rates evolve; always validate with a mortgage broker. Each chapter ends with a lined « My notes » page.

chapters.title: 1 to 4 units vs 5 units and more
chapters.objective: Understand the key dividing line in rental financing.
chapters.html:
Understand the key dividing line in rental financing.

The fundamental distinction: buildings of 1 to 4 units are financed under rules close to residential, whereas buildings of 5 units and more are considered « commercial » (multi-unit), with different rules, a different down payment, and a different analysis, centred on the building's profitability.

  • 1 to 4 units: lower down payment, especially if you occupy one unit.
  • 5 units and more: higher down payment, analysis based on the building's NOI.
  • The 5-unit threshold changes your structure considerably.
Emilie's tip

Going from 4 to 5 units changes everything on the financing side. If you are starting out, a building of 4 units or fewer is often the most accessible entry point.

chapters.title: The down payment and owner-occupancy
chapters.objective: Optimize the down payment for your project.
chapters.html:
Optimize the down payment for your project.

For a 1-to-4-unit building that you occupy, the down payment can be significantly reduced (see the owner-occupant guide). For a non-occupied rental building, the required down payment is generally higher.

  • Owner-occupant (1-4 units): reduced down payment, better terms.
  • Non-occupant investor: larger down payment.
  • Part of the rental income can help you qualify for your loan.
Emilie's tip

If your situation allows it, occupying one unit of your first plex unlocks much more advantageous financing. It is often the best springboard to get started.

chapters.title: Loan insurance and the treatment of rental income
chapters.objective: Understand the role of insurance programs.
chapters.html:
Understand the role of insurance programs.

Loan insurers (CMHC and others) offer multi-unit programs that can allow a reduced down payment and better terms, in exchange for a premium. The building's rental income is taken into account in the analysis, to varying degrees.

These programs and their criteria evolve: a mortgage broker who specializes in income properties is your best ally for identifying the best option.

Emilie's tip

Work with a mortgage broker who is used to rental property. The right insurance program or the right lender can turn a marginal project into a profitable one.

chapters.title: Building a solid structure
chapters.html:
Assemble financing that protects profitability.

  • Compare several lenders (rates AND terms, penalties, flexibility).
  • Build in a cushion: if rates rise at renewal, does the project still hold?
  • Keep liquidity for unexpected costs and repairs.
  • Think ahead: a good structure makes the next purchase easier (refinancing).

Financing is not just a formality: it is a strategic lever that determines your cash flow and your ability to grow.

Emilie's tip

Don't just chase the lowest rate: think about flexibility and the ability to refinance. Your first structure should open the door to your second building.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, in concrete terms.

This week

  1. Determine the number of units and my status (occupant or not).
  2. Meet with a mortgage broker who specializes in rental property.

Within 30 days

  1. Compare programs and lenders (rates and terms).
  2. Structure the financing with a cushion for rate increases.

Then

  1. Secure financing that protects cash flow and growth.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• 1-4 units: a financing regime close to residential.
  • 5 units and more: multi-unit « commercial », analysis based on NOI.
  • Down payment: lower if owner-occupant, higher if a pure investor.
  • Multi-unit loan insurance: programs (CMHC, etc.) with a reduced down payment, for a premium.
  • Refinancing: a lever to finance the next purchase.
